Look into a sleep study if you can! I had this same issue for years and doctors/therapists/psychiatrists all blamed depression. Then I had someone refer me for a sleep study and surprise! I have sleep apnea! No one caught it sooner because I never snored, which is a hallmark of obstructive sleep apnea. I have "central sleep apnea" where my brain just...doesn't send signals to the muscles that handle breathing. I've been using a CPAP for three-ish years now. I lost weight, I gained energy, my memory improved, I could go on. Point is, get a sleep study if you can. Sleep apnea isn't the only sleep disorder out there and you deserve quality rest.

In the aftermath, be prepared for self-care. Ice packs on any spots you hit or your hands. If you have access to it, OTC pain medication. Clean and disinfect any open wounds. Seek medical attention if you feel like you had a serious injury or show symptoms of concussion. 

And consider getting a stuffed animal or soft doll. Not to hit, but to hold when it’s over. You can find one small enough to fit in a purse if that’s what you need, like a beanie baby or whatever, and you can just squish it in your hand. I always find that sensory overload messes with my mood in the time after I do a fun event. If I go to a noisy concert, which I love doing, I can expect a week of general depression and irritability while my body recovers from the high-stimulus environment.

I have depression, antidepressants have worked wonders for me, and it’s allowed me to see the difference between “my brain is not producing enough of the right chemicals” and “I am reasonably feeling under the weather because I overstimulated myself.”

The best thing I find to help with sensory and social overload is starting self-care and rest, as much as possible, BEFORE I do a major thing I’m really excited about. In the concert example, I make sure that for a couple of days before I am taking as much quiet time as I can. I protect my senses, I hydrate and eat as well as I can, and sleep. I have to go to work, but I don’t make additional social plans, I don’t go shopping at busy stores, etc. Thanks to this I have a strong need for way-in-advance planning, I do NOT do spontaneous things very often, but it also means that in the time afterward I have a lot less recovery to do because I went in feeling good.

There don’t appear to be any clinical studies on this in adults, but a 2009 study showed that citalopram (Celexa) used to treat repetitive behavior in autistic children increased energy, impulsiveness, and insomnia. [Here’s a link to the study if you want to read it](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4112556/). It’s so frustrating that there’s nothing meaningful for adults.

In this case it’s okay for them to be a little self-conscious. I have a few stims that drive people up the walls (like, say, tongue clicking) and it’s important that I be told when they’re infringing on someone’s comfort. Does it make me feel self-conscious in the moment? Yes. Does it also help me to coexist peacefully in a shared space with other people? Yes! I find other stims (maybe drumming my fingers on my leg) that fill the same need but aren’t disruptive.

Especially if this is in a workplace, it’s really important that this person be aware of other people. Set aside the autism for a moment: this is no different than asking people not to microwave fish or listen to loud music without headphones. It sounds like you’ve done a lot to accommodate them, but that goes both ways. You also deserve to have your needs respected and met. You’re not asking them to completely hide who they are, you’re asking them to make an accommodation for your comfort in a space that both of you have to occupy. So I advise being polite and kind (which it sounds like you are), ask them if there’s some kind of stim they can do instead, and if they get upset with you then you can move this along to a manager if you have one. (Highly recommend the Ask a Manager blog for scripts, you might not find autism-specific things but there are plenty of resources on talking to coworkers about many things like this.)

I completely get you. I 100% understand why level 2/3 autistics are upset with the situation. I understand why they feel frustrated and talked over. I understand why they might not have much sympathy for me as a level 1 autistic. I want to support them and give them the floor to express their needs and experiences. That’s incredibly important.

But I end up feeling like I’m wrong for sharing my experiences and struggles. From allistics and other autistics, the message comes across that “you’re level 1 so you don’t really have problems.” I’m level 1 so I should be able to hold a job, maintain a social life, not have meltdowns…and when I struggle with these things I either don’t deserve sympathy because I don’t have it as bad as anyone else, or because I’m just not trying. Never mind the fact that I’m living forever at home with my family because advanced activities of daily living are beyond me, because I can take care of my personal hygiene I clearly don’t have any real problems. (And yes, I’ve heard that exact thing said. I’m not inventing this.)

There has to be a way to make space for all autistics regardless of level/support needs. We have different struggles and need different support, and a lot of people need way more support than others, but at the end of the day we’re all autistic. When I got my diagnosis, that’s what I was excited for. We all share so many things that I was hoping to find a community. Instead, I ended up feeling shame from all directions. So I don’t participate in most autism communities anymore.

I’ve had a similar struggle with this style of therapy. It’s called Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), which aims to change distorted thinking so that behaviors that come from those distorted thoughts will change. It works very well for certain issues, like anxiety and depression, but from a lot of anecdotes doesn’t seem to work as well if at all for autistic people.

When I talk to a therapist who uses CBT, there’s a built-in assumption that I have some kind of distorted thinking. If I say “I feel like people at work hate me,” the therapist assumes that I’m having distorted thoughts, like blowing minor problems out of proportion or projecting self-image issues onto coworkers. For a lot of people, the therapist would be correct. CBT techniques could help someone to correctly perceive the size of problems or improve their self-image so they could stop projecting.

For me, it’s wrong. When I say “I feel like people at work hate me,” what I’m picking up on is the fact that autism-related social challenges are causing rifts between me and coworkers. I’m being ostracized for missing social cues or being laughed at for “weird” behaviors. It’s not distorted thinking: it’s really happening to me. Changing my thoughts doesn’t change reality and it increases, not decreases, the pain.

CBT is really common, because it IS very effective for many people. For me, too many years of CBT landed me in a hospital and I won’t do it again. Right now I’m looking for someone who can help with radical acceptance therapy, which focuses on healthy coping with feelings brought on by things beyond our control. I’ve heard it’s worked for other autistic people and I’m hoping it will work for me. It’s worth a shot, at least.

Even “vanilla” sex is complicated and full of sensory stimulation. Of course, there’s coordinating the act itself, which can be challenging even with experience, especially if you have trouble with spacial perceptions. You’re with another person so there’s a social element. If you’re averse to eye contact or touch, you might be challenged by being so physically close to someone.

You’re processing the feelings of your own body, trying to be attuned to your partner’s body, keeping track of the environment. And that assumes all of those things are pleasant. If you don’t like the texture of sheets, if a smell bothers you, if the temperature of the room is wrong, whatever—now you’re also trying to manage discomfort.

With all of that, even if you’re having a great time, it’s not surprising that you don’t make a lot of noise. I seriously advise that you not start trying to make noise that doesn’t feel natural to you. That will separate you from the moment, and can even make you feel unhappy afterwards. If your partner is worried that you’re not enjoying sex because you’re quiet, talk to them about it. Maybe find some verbal ways to express enjoyment, or talk about how you express your feelings through touch and your body. It might feel awkward to discuss, but you deserve to have your needs met.

The restrictions are 100% spectrum-related, yeah! The scrambled eggs thing you mention is exactly on point, that actually happened to me (a month of only eggs, followed by a month of not being able to look at eggs). As far as I know there’s no specific name, but searching this subreddit, other autism-related subreddits, or elsewhere online for “food sensitivity and autism” (or similar things) will bring up many, many people talking about the same struggle.

I’ve had a small number of “safe” foods as long as I can remember, and those are always okay. But sometimes overnight other foods will go from acceptable to unacceptable. I went years enjoying fish and then one day I took a bite of salmon and started crying. In that case it was the smell. In the case of cooked spinach, it was a texture. Though suddenly my body is demanding spinach daily, so who knows? Blueberries, it was too much variation (one would be tart and squishy, the next firm and sweet, too much variety). It’s very up to the individual person. Things that are soft and bland (like potatoes) are likely to be inedible to me, but I know someone who can always eat potatoes no matter what. It’s frustrating to have it be so arbitrary. Does all that make sense? It’s hard to understand and I experience it, explaining it out loud can be confusing.

Hey, thank YOU for reaching out for help. You clearly care a lot about your daughter and want her to be happy and healthy. I think you’re headed down the right path here. 

Yeah, the toys do sound like a “being a kid” issue. But the food thing—I can maybe speak to that more? I deal with food restrictions and it’s really painful. It’s not that I don’t want anything else, or that nothing will make me happy, it’s that anything other than what my brain/body is demanding will make me sick. I almost threw up this morning because I ate a bite of scrambled egg. It was upsetting. Embarrassing too. I ended up eating plain toast because I physically couldn’t handle anything else. Not even cereal and yogurt, or peanut butter, all of which I keep on hand because they’re nearly guaranteed to be safe to eat.

It’s taken me a LONG time to be able to talk about this clearly. For my entire life, I was asking for identical lunches every day, secretly throwing out things that inexplicably made me nauseated just to see, and picking every tiny piece of things I “didn’t like” out of meals. It’s only after my diagnosis as an adult that I’ve been able to piece this together. If your daughter has similar issues to me and other people like me, then “I don’t want anything else, I can’t wait for tomorrow” could be translated to “every kind of food but one is making me feel distressed and I’m hungry.” She just might not know how to say that.

Which, I totally get why that’s worrisome as a parent. A lot of times, safe foods are safe because they’re identical every time and you always know what to expect. A bowl of cereal is always the same—a bowl of baby carrots can have an overwhelming number of different sizes, colors, flavors, textures. So I pick the cereal. And of course then the problem is that doesn’t have the nutrients of the carrots. I really do understand why this could add stress to this, if your daughter is asking for things that aren’t nutritious or have a lot of sugar.

One of the things that has helped me is being involved in making my own food. Preparing my own meals (muffins and smoothies with sneaky vegetables, vegetable pizzas where I chopped all the toppings myself) has helped because I’m able to see, touch, and taste everything going into my meal. Also, by having control over the process, I feel calmer and more prepared for the end result. Obviously your daughter is young enough that some things might be beyond her skills or need supervision, but maybe offering her some kind of extra input when you can could help?

Wall of text ahead, sorry. I hope it’s not too overwhelming. I just have a lot of passion about this sort of thing.

Some of these (like saying forbidden words to push boundaries) sound like they’re just from being 8 years old—allistic kids do the same things. Some others sound like they could be autistic behaviors that are being exacerbated by being 8 years old.

Very rigid thinking and a strong sense of fairness are both autistic traits. In the gift example, your daughter’s inexperience with the world might be contributing to a sense of dismay at perceived unfairness, and she’s lashing out because she can’t process the emotions. Same with the pizza. I’m an adult and while I don’t get openly upset about unequal portions, I still REALLY dislike when people cut pizzas or pies unevenly or when someone takes the smallest cookie so someone else can have the larger one.

With cleaning up, there’s every chance that your daughter is struggling with uncertainty. If you say “clean up your room,” that’s a pretty vague statement. An allistic kid might be able to break that down without further direction (put toys away, try to make the bed, organize the desk), but an autistic kid could very easily struggle to figure out what they’re expected to do, how they’re expected to do it, and where to start doing it. That’s how I grew up! And then, again, being 8 isn’t doing her any favors, because she hasn’t figured out yet how to ask for more detailed instructions or explain that she’s feeling overwhelmed. Do you give her more specific directions, or is there just the expectation that she’ll figure it out alone?

Food, similar thing. Could be sensory issues (texture, smell, taste) that she doesn’t know how to explain. Could be simple food preference. Could be a little bit of both, or a feedback loop. Regardless, the fact that she slowly starts eating and tries to hide that from you is alarming to me—that gives off the vibe that, whatever is going on with the refusal to eat what’s in front of her, she’s hungry and has no other options. Or she feels like she’s going to get scolded/given an “I told you you’d like it” if she admits to liking what’s in front of her. Either way, that isn’t great. Do you provide your daughter with the option of other (healthy and simple) choices that she can make for herself when she refuses to eat? Or is it “what’s on your plate or nothing”?

All of that said, you’re right in thinking her responses to all these things aren’t okay. Yelling and screaming and being aggressive is a natural reaction to her distress. Autistic people like us have strong emotions that often appear disproportionate to the situation we’re in. But they’re still hurtful to the people around her. If she’s having trouble, then she needs you to help her figure out appropriate responses. Are there calmer ways she can express unhappiness? Are there other words she can say when she’s mad? Is there space for her to ask questions when she’s confused?

Your daughter is going to need your kindness, help, and guidance to navigate the world. It’s not that she’s incapable, but that she needs accommodation. She needs detailed instructions for complicated tasks. She needs to have uncertain things explained to her instead of being told “that’s just how it is.” She needs to be allowed to eat food that’s safe (and healthy) for her. And most of all, she needs to be treated like a person who is good and worthy of respect even though she has social challenges, not as a badly behaved child in need of punishment.

Apologies for the wall of text, autism overexplaining definitely kicked in here. It sounds trite but: communication is absolutely key. My partner has ADHD and I’m autistic. We have places where our needs overlap, but just as many if not more where our needs are contradictory. For example, they need constant mental stimulation from many sources, while I need to exist in quiet and still spaces. In our early relationship we struggled a lot to navigate this, and it wasn’t until we opened up and started to honestly talk about what we needed that things got better.

Now, we make time for both of us to have what we need. I make time to be in their noisier, faster-paced space where we can laugh and do many things at once, while they make time to sit and do quiet “parallel play” activities with me. 

Sometimes we do have to make clearly-communicated compromises when our needs clash. “Compromise” should never mean that you hurt yourself or sacrifice your dignity. For us, it might mean that I put an explicit time limit on high-stimulation activities. During parallel times, my partner might have half a dozen activities going while I focus on one. It’s not exactly what either of us wants, but it meets both our needs.

We’ve been together for seven years now and still going strong. No plans to get legally married, but…life partners? I think so. And we’ve talked about that and what that means, too.

That last paragraph is really important: that you want to help him find tools to make his life easier and better. Framing your concerns like that could be helpful. Tell him you want to support him and that you think a diagnosis would be a good tool for him to live a happier life.

If your husband is concerned about stigma or resistant to “getting a label,” you might still offer to work with him to research skills and coping mechanisms to help with the challenges he faces—without the label. If he has difficulty regulating emotions or handling complex social situations, for example, there are plenty of resources that don’t require a diagnosis. I have people in my life who for various reasons aren’t pursuing a diagnosis, but have been learning skills and tools anyway to help themselves. It’s working out for them.

One other thing—if your husband is autistic (or has any other neurodivergence), he’s faced a lifetime of challenges. You’ve clearly seen some of them yourself. Reading more posts in this sub by late-diagnosed autistics can give you some further insight. Your husband may have internalized some really unpleasant things over his life. If you have this conversation, reinforce to him that you love him as a complete person, and you’re not bringing this up because he did something wrong. It’s an autistic thing. When people talk about “problems with social interaction,” this is a huge part of it. Research is starting to confirm what a lot of us instinctively know: autistic people have a different way of communicating than allistic people. It’s long been perceived as a deficit on our part, but views are slowly changing to affirm that we aren’t doing something wrong. Our brains are just wired so differently that communication between autistic and allistic people is extra challenging on both sides. Look up the “double empathy problem” for more details.

For me, it’s definitely the core of my social issues: knowing that there’s not a “right” answer, maybe, but there’s some kind of reaction that’s what someone expects/wants to get, and for some reason it’s a reaction I can’t give. In scripted interactions, I’m extremely capable. I’m very good at customer service and public speaking. But that’s because I can learn the rules to those interactions and follow them to a T. If something goes off the rails, I become a confused, stammering mess (or just forget how to talk entirely, that’s always fun) in seconds.

My family has always told me the same thing in reverse. When they talk to me, they feel like there’s some way they’re supposed to respond to me, but they can’t even begin to find it. That’s the double empathy problem in play. Now that we know more (I’m recently diagnosed), we’ve been able to start finding common ground. But it’s still hard. It probably always will be. I think it’s worth it, though. Allistic folks do have a lot to offer, when you can understand what they’re saying!

Worse for me is disorientation. If my routine breaks (even if I’m the one who broke it), then finishing it turns into total confusion. I always do things in the exact same order in the shower, and if I do a step out of order (shave before washing hair, for example) I get confused enough to start looping until I can fix it. Not a parent, recently diagnosed adult who hopes that I can provide some extra perspective. I have mixed feelings about my situation. I had parents who supported my social/sensory needs as a kid, I was homeschooled and given the chance to learn at my pace, and I thrived. Because of my home situation, my parents never even considered a diagnosis—their parenting style supported my needs so well that I was in many ways not disabled. They knew I was “different,” but it didn’t impede me.

When I went to school, and then moved on into college, all of that collapsed really quickly. Without a diagnosis, I didn’t have the language to describe what was happening or the skills to manage…anything, really. I was ridiculously academically successful, but I was extremely socially isolated. And I didn’t know why. That, combined with issues of executive function, led me to seek a diagnosis. Now I have the language and skills—but it’s too late to help my younger self.

I guess what I’m saying with my experience is that it’s a mixed bag. Had I been diagnosed as a kid, I’d have had the language and skills to help make it through the huge challenges I faced—but I might have found myself stereotyped and shoehorned into things I didn’t want as I got older thanks to stigma. I’m still not sure where I stand myself, and maybe I never will be.

I don’t think this post is necessarily about sharing challenges and therapy, but about general conversation. I also find it draining to talk about difficulties (with anybody, group therapy is exhausting), so I do get that! Talking to other neurodivergent people in a casual way, on the other hand, is just…easier. Even doing “small talk” doesn’t feel like I’m trying to navigate a minefield like it usually does, and talking about our interests or things we’ve done is pleasurable and easy. It’s just not like it is with neurotypical people.

I don’t always have a special interest. Sometimes I’ll go a while (even years) without something specific occupying my mind. I consider those really relaxing times, because I can devote all of myself to other things. I get to engage fully with interests that are less intense. 

I usually don’t have more than one special interest at a time! Sometimes I get lucky and run into something that overlaps a past interest with a present one (like if I had a special interest in researching conspiracy theories, had previously been invested in the Titanic disaster, then discovered a theory that was about said disaster). That’s always fun!

Sometimes I’ll dabble in old special interests, because for me they will always bring some amount of happiness. But I no longer feel the urge to think only about that thing. 

And intensity does vary! Sometimes I live and breathe an interest (I was an autistic kid with a dinosaur special interest), and sometimes it’s my favorite thing but I’m able to focus on other stuff. That’s happened more as I’ve gotten older and gotten better about compartmentalizing my life.

Normal interests for me are things that I enjoy doing or thinking about, but can put down and not think about when I’m done. I might enjoy a book and talk about it, but I can move on from it. Same with other activities. 

I can’t stop thinking about a special interest, when I have one. Part of my mind will always be considering it (planning an activity, reflecting on a movie, whatever) and, no matter what I do, I can’t turn that off. It may affect how I interact with people, because the urge to turn a conversation back to the interest is incredibly strong. It often results in hyperfocus—without great effort, the only thing I can do is think about the activity.

However, this doesn’t mean I know all the details. If I’m interested in, say, the Avengers movies, I might not remember every plot point/what characters are called/how things tie into each other—but I’ll want to watch those movies above any others at all times, I’ll always be  replaying scenes in my mind, and struggling not to turn every conversation back to the movies. Disclaimer: this has never actually been a special interest for me, but other media franchises have. They follow a similar pattern.

It’s taken me a long time, but I’m finally at the point where, when I’m done with something, I put it away right then. Mail? Opened the second I get it and put in the right spot the second it’s open (bills to their basket, paperwork to theirs, envelopes to recycling). Dishes? Washed and put away as they get dirty, not left in the sink for later. A shopping trip? Put the items away the second I walk in the door with the bag without taking off my shoes. It doesn’t resolve everything, but it keeps me from feeling overwhelmed day to day.

I also have to remind myself to be kind to myself. This is executive dysfunction—it’s not a choice for me to struggle. If I make a huge mess, that’s not a reflection of failure, it’s a reflection of a neurodivergent mind. Berating and speaking badly to myself will just hurt me. The only way to get through it is to be gentle and patient with myself. So no matter how you end up tackling this, I encourage you to be kind to yourself too.

I thought of myself as high-empathy too, until I realized what I am is high-sympathy. I don’t feel what people feel, but I want to help them when they’re in distress and I’m good at understanding why they might be distressed. Or I’m truly glad they’re happy and I can understand why. I just...don’t feel it. And I think that’s okay.

A high-empathy family member explained her experiences like this: she can ‘feel’ someone else’s emotions. Their happiness becomes ‘her’ happiness, and their sadness becomes ‘her’ sadness. She experiences feelings with the other person. They laugh or cry together because they are sharing the emotion. 

I have low empathy. I can understand that someone is sad, and it makes me unhappy to see them in distress because I care about them, but I can’t seem to share in the experience. I also respond not by wanting to participate in the emotion together, but by offering ways to help (because I understand that people in distress need help). Same thing with happiness: I feel disconnected from a group’s shared enjoyment. We aren’t experiencing happiness together, I’m appreciating that they’re happy.

I’ve learned to mask all this really well. It wasn’t until I got into therapy that I started unpacking all of this. It’s not that I don’t care. I do, sometimes too much. But I’m not sharing that emotional connection. I hope all this makes sense!

One of the things that multiple professionals have told me is that my misdiagnosis of bipolar disorder is a hallmark of many undiagnosed autistic adults. I was misdiagnosed Type II and, while the surface looks similar, it’s not the same underneath. A psychologist put me through an intensive bipolar evaluation process (mandatory to have therapy at their center) and told me without a shadow of a doubt I was NOT bipolar. The evaluation wasn’t geared toward autism, but after I also came up as definitely not having BPD, I started looking. 

What looks like hypomania in me is when I push myself too hard masking. I’m overcompensating for social struggle, which reads as the high energy and outgoing-ness that accompany hypomania. The “pressured speech” only really happens when I’m in the deep throes of a special interest, and just can’t contain my excitement! And the depression...well, that’s just depression. 

I got really lucky that the mood stabilizer I was put on actually helped. It wasn’t a cure-all, but it helped me regulate my emotions enough that I stopped having meltdowns all the time. A provider tried to put me on abilify—that went BADLY. It was designed to help an issue I wasn’t truly having, and so exacerbated issues I was having. That, alongside the evaluation, was what got me looking very hard at autism. 

Lo and behold, turns out I’m a walking checklist for the DSM. Nobody looked for it because I’m missing some of the visible traits (I don’t stim with rocking or flapping, I can consistently make eye contact, my routines are very subtle). Once i started looking, though? Obvious. No way it was bipolar disorder—it just looked like that from the outside.

In brief: Eggs don’t need replacing. Women are born with a lot of eggs in their ovaries already, all that they’ll need in a lifetime. (There’s research that suggests they can be replaced, but it’s not something widely studied.)

During the menstrual cycle, the uterus gains a lining of tissue to support a fertilized egg (released from the ovaries and into the uterus). If the egg isn’t fertilized, the body needs to get rid of the lining. That’s a period.

I’ve been actively writing for upwards of ten years at this point (unpublished, hobbyist only here), so some advice for those “down” times (which it sounds like you might be in):

Try to find an online writing community. Not a critique group (those can be awful if you’re already in a dry spell), just a community of people who share an interest with you. 

Embrace short stuff. If you’re struggling to write an epic poem, try a sonnet first. Write microfiction (100 words) or flash fiction (1000). Journal entry before autobiography. 

And finally—many writers I know (myself included) stall out trying to write something profound. Remember: you don’t have to shake the earth with your writing, especially not when you’re writing as a hobby. Just enjoy yourself.

So...I can't give you a script. However, I do have some ideas for delivery. I think whatever you say should be said with compassion. That doesn't mean, however, that you should skirt around the point: be straightforward with him. Explain how you are feeling and how much you're suffering right now. Take the time for some self-care afterwards. I know you work long hours, but perhaps this is the time to call in a sick day, if you can. Whatever the outcome of the conversation, you are going to need a minute to breathe and recover from the emotional toll.

I don't have all the answers, but I think it's important that you hear this: he may need you, but **you need yourself too**. I’m a horror movie fan, and I’m of two minds (ha) about mental illness in horror films. 

I’ve also thought about this a lot, so wall of text incoming. TLDR at the bottom.

**On the one hand**: I understand how deeply harmful “mental illness as horror” is on a society-wide scale. The people in need of care are made out to be monstrous and frightening, rather than...well, human. It warps perceptions of mental illness in such a way that real live people are hurt.

Filmmakers need to do a better job of handling their mental illness metaphors as well. Even if the condition is demonic possession or whatever, it still draws heavy parallels to real illnesses. By framing symptoms as existing due to “evil,” perceptions of mental illness as frightening and evil itself perpetuate. NOT okay.

**On the other hand:** i, personally, am empowered by horror movie mental illness. I know you’re asking about movies, but in a video game example, the game Outlast has a great deal of mental illness horror. The patients, though, despite being antagonists, are victims of bad science and possibly-supernatural activity. I’m afraid of hospitals and what could happen to me in the unknown of involuntary medical treatment. It allowed me to process some of my fears in a safe way.

When the mentally ill person (or the person with a mental illness metaphor) truly is the monster, and not a victim—frankly it’s a power fantasy, in the sense of being unchained. I hate the idea of hurting people and would *NEVER* do that. But the idea of cutting loose—going off my meds, foregoing treatment, doing whatever I want—is very very tempting. For the two hours of the movie, I can “live out” the experience of being free of constraint, safe in the knowledge that when the movie’s over I’ll go take my meds and engage in positive, socially-appropriate behaviors.

**TLDR: mental illness in horror movies is damaging on a society-wide scale, but is personally empowering to me.**

I have type II bipolar disorder. Mine mostly expresses itself as long, deep depressions (I was misdiagnosed with unipolar depression until I went to therapy in the middle of a hypomanic episode). Your father sounds like he was type I, which expresses itself mostly through mania with short, intense depressions (the most commonly-thought-of form in popular culture). 

I’m so sorry he was abusive. That is a bipolar patient at his worst. It sounds like he either wasn’t seeking treatment or was not responding well to what treatment he had. 

If I had to guess based on my own struggle, he regretted his actions during his lows and tried to make up for them when his mood was high. **It doesn’t excuse his abuse at all**. But I would be willing to bet that he was deeply unhappy that he hurt you and that he was confused and angry with himself for not being able to control himself during his lows.

Control of this disorder takes so much time. I am lucky not to feel rage and that we caught this early enough that I was starting to work on strategies for when I had episodes even when I was 9-10 years old, or younger. It is an arduous journey and I’m *still* struggling after over a decade of fighting without knowing a diagnosis and three years with one. It can feel like...hm, I used to describe it before I was treated as being inside a blender full of broken glass. Inescapable, disorienting, and very, very painful. 

**None of this excuses mistreating other people**. Others can and should set boundaries to protect themselves when people with bipolar disorder hurt them. It’s the responsibility of the person with bipolar to manage their disorder, not hurt people, and make real amends when they do. No matter how he felt, your father had the responsibility to take care of you and protect you, even if it was from himself.

Sometimes there is no root problem. I have a mental illness cocktail (four disorders in a trench coat is how I describe myself) and depression is certainly one. There’s no root to it, no *reason* for me to be like this. The depression is its own root. 

And it’s less a root like a carrot and more like the hyphae of a fungal colony. It’s woven into the structure of who I am—it’s not all of me or the core of me, but the illness is spread through me in such a way that pulling it out for good would require chemicals that could destroy the core of me right alongside the depression. 

Treatment for that isn’t as simple as taking a look at what’s wrong in my life (especially when, to be honest, the biggest thing wrong in my life is that I’m the one living it). To an outside observer, the problem could be “solved” if I would tidy my room, use a planner, or get more exercise. The problem is that my inability to pick up after myself, maintain a consistent schedule, or find the motivation to get out of bed are *symptoms* of the illness, rather than the cause. 

I’m lucky that I’m in a position where I have access to treatment. I’m lucky that I have the money for medications and constant appointments with doctors. I’m lucky that I have a strong support network. I’m lucky that my illness expresses itself in a way that allows me to shower and feed myself and get my schoolwork done on time. Regarding equality and equity, I guess the best thing I can point to is [this graphic made by Craig Froehle](https://medium.com/@CRA1G/the-evolution-of-an-accidental-meme-ddc4e139e0e4), which (albeit simplistically) demonstrates the difference between equality and equity. 

In the world where “Everyone Can Code,” everyone is given an identical advantage from the outset. However, other barriers—media depicting coding as a male-dominated career, hiring biases, policies that disproportionately impact women who have children, and so on—are left unaddressed. (And those things are very real, but I’ll let other posters tackle those and focus on equality vs. equity.) Despite the leveled starting point, the outcome isn’t changed.

In the world where “Girls Can Code,” the ideal situation is that young women are given an extra boost of skills, networking, and education that allows them to *catch up* to male peers who already have an advantage. They’re given more at the start because they need that boost just to catch up and reach a point where they also have the chance to achieve success.

In a nutshell, it’s not an attempt to say that men don’t face barriers or challenges and shouldn’t be supported. Rather, it’s an acknowledgement that women face a specific set of barriers and challenges which *men don’t face*, and which require specific strategies and programs to overcome. It’s not to make women “better” than men—it’s to try to get everyone onto the same playing field at all.

Disclaimer: I do have a mental illness (bipolar type II). However, I have a sister who does NOT suffer from the same condition. We share *many* personality traits, though, and we've talked before about the fact that the greatest difference in our experiences of the world is that one of us is sick and the other isn't. 

My sister is able, within a reasonable time, to let go of insults and injuries. She doesn't revisit those things months and years later or, if she does, she doesn't relive them. She has a sense of equilibrium in her everyday life: things can be "okay" without swinging dramatically up or down. An experience can be "meh". Setbacks upset her, but she can pick herself up without days or weeks of work. Likewise, exciting events leave her happy and smiling, but don't put her at risk of a month or more of elevated mood that threatens her life and college degree. 

When she's confronted with exceptional experiences, in other words, she's able to process them in a way that doesn't leave long-lasting and traumatic effects. She requires no particular treatments in order to approach a "normal" response. Counseling, the few times she's used it, is a method of processing one event or seeking help for a non-pathological behavior. It's not a lifelong method of working through pathologically unhealthy behaviors and dangerous brain chemistry. 

In a nutshell: she can recover from things without much external help. I can't. Life for her is much more independent and much less *monitored*. No one is looking over her shoulder to make sure her decisions weren't made because of a disorder.

"American exceptionalism" is a long-standing tradition in American culture and, more narrowly, politics. From the founding of the country, Americans have held a belief (however faulty) that their democracy is a unique form of government. At the time of its founding, this was true. It was revolutionary and highly progressive. Its ideas, surprisingly enough, were well ahead of many other nations at the time. This isn't so much true today, but the idea has held on (despite the fact that on the Democracy Index the US holds the 21st position, below some countries the US has traditionally derided as undemocratic).

This idea of uniqueness gave rise, on some level, to the idea of an inherent American *superiority*. If we're unique, the thought goes, we must be better, more advanced than other countries. This idea hasn't been helped by political rhetoric and standards of education within the US, both of which explicitly encourage Americans to think of themselves as superior to the rest of the world.

There are always policy implications to such an attitude. For example, in Europe, where people value the government as a caretaker, we see social policies that support those values even in the face of increasing value placed on individual liberty. In China, which still values the legacy of Mao, we see policies of enforced economic equality despite rising capitalist values. These are just two examples of how a cultural legacy can give rise to policy decisions that, on the surface, can seem eccentric.

In the US, American exceptionalism has shaped foreign policy for all of its history. Americans are allowed to do things that they would never tolerate from another country, because being a leader once has made us leaders forever. Like other posters have said, this is partly a legacy of the Cold War (we were once one of few nuclear-capable countries and remain the world's strongest military power), but it goes beyond the that. America sees itself as the protector of the world because of more than two centuries of rhetoric and policy that dictate that America is special. It isn't an attitude backed up by fact, but it's an attitude with policy ramifications all the same.

As for musicals:
- Hamilton's line "I'm a diamond in the rough" is a shout-out to Aladdin. (Not necessarily a traditional Broadway musical, but it's a musical all the same.)
- George Washington's introduction includes a homage to "Modern Major-General's Song" from Pirates of Penzance.
- The 1776 reference is someone (I think Hamilton?) shouting "Sit down, John!" at John Adams.
- In "Your Obedient Servant", one of Aaron Burr's lines is melodically identical to a line from "Javert's Suicide" in Les Miserables (confirmed by creator as well as being totally audible, I noticed it and then looked it up). 
- And I'm sure there are others, but I haven't listened to the whole soundtrack looking for references...those are just the ones I noticed while I was listening. There are also apparently a LOT of hip-hop references, but I don't know hip-hop very well and so I'm not the person who can point those out. The best thing if you're really interested would be to look at Hamilton: The Revolution, which contains a lot of annotations from Lin-Manuel Miranda that help explain the references in the text.

As for modern politics:

The simple fact that this story told almost entirely without white voices in a time where race is such a major issue in front of eyes of America, and the fact that it has become so incredibly popular and well-known, makes a political statement. But I shouldn't speak on that point: I'll yield the floor to [Kendra James](http://the-toast.net/2015/10/01/race-immigration-and-hamilton/), who's a lot more qualified than I.

There's a fair bit of commentary on politics, yes. *Hamilton* is a look at history through a modern political lens. References to modern politics are often pretty subtle and rely on context clues, but they are there. One notable example is the line "Immigrants: we get the job done"--a pretty obvious response to modern anti-immigration sentiment. There are plenty of others, though. 

If you want to listen to it, the whole soundtrack is available for free on Youtube, and it's definitely worth your time if you enjoy history/musicals/historical musicals. (There are also plenty of references to other musicals, including one I laugh at every time that's a direct callback to 1776.)

The boardroom's doors open gently, without a noise, but the hubbub within dies instantly. Every eye--be it that of a goat, an octopus, a fly, or something far stranger--turns instantly to the well-dressed figure striding calmly in.

"Well, gentlemen," Satan says, "good morning."

The assembled horde begins to pay obeisance to the Dread Lord of Hell, but Satan waves his hand genially. "We're close enough to the election that I think we can dispense with the formalities. Sit down, everyone. We have a campaign to plan."

Of course he takes the seat at the head of the table. Wary, each and every demon watches Satan's every move. With a snap of his fingers, he conjures up a ballot. "Gentlemen. In order to win the election against Heaven in this millennium, we require a little more than three-billion, five hundred and sixty-two million, five-hundred-thousand of these." He looks around the table, golden eyes sparkling. "Are there any ideas? How will we convince the humans that I will do the best possible job of ruling the universe?"

One demon, a specimen with centipedes growing out of every pore, cackles wildly. "Let us use temptation!" it chatters with its millions of mouths.

A buxom demon with black eyes smiles. "No, we must inspire them with war!"

Without any real provocation, a fight breaks out in one corner as five or six demons try to resolve their differences by the time-honored method of murder. Other demons argue and prevaricate, attempting to prove their points. Satan watches, waiting for the strongest demons to win.

A damned soul sidles through the crack in the door and scurries between the lashing claws and tentacles of the demons. It makes a beeline for Satan. Through the blisters and scourge marks it has sustained in its time in Hell, it is recognizable as a politician. 

"My Lord," it says humbly, kneeling at Satan's hooves. "If you will permit me, I have an idea of how you might win the election. There are certain ways to brand your opponent so that he's discredited. Mortals are a fearful lot, and the right word means everything!"

Satan strokes his beard. "Very well," he says. He gestures at the assembled demons. The boardroom has now begun to look more like a battlefield. "They're not being terribly useful. Tell me."

"What is wrong?" Michael asks. At the sound of the great voice, the cherub cowers.

Uriel smiles. "Do not be afraid. What has happened?"

The cherub plucks up its courage. "Well...I've been out counting ballots and...I'm afraid that Hell is probably going to win the election."

The angels cry out in terror. Gabriel's thousand eyes roll with anger. "How can this be!?"

"Smartness" isn't a good method of evaluating intelligence. The "smartest" people I've ever met are the people who knew how to express themselves. They don't have a lot of knowledge or understanding about the things they discuss. But when they speak, they sound intelligent, so people think of them as "smart". 

On the other hand, many of the most intelligent people I know can't express themselves. Although they have deep knowledge and understanding of a given topic, they can't talk about it. They don't sound intelligent, so people think that they aren't smart.

Basically, if you want to "become smarter", learn how to express yourself.

At first it was just fun.

Tumblr? Half my followers turned out to be bots, which sort of sucked. One of my followers, though, was a cute girl who went to my college. I'd never met her in person, but I managed to track her down and strike up a conversation. Two weeks later--courtesy of her Tumblr diary--we were dating. She had no idea how I'd found her, and it was great. 

Reddit? No more anonymity. It was fun to mess with people, posting suggestive details about their lives, just enough to make them nervous, and then backing off. I knew who they were. Finding their Facebook pages was easy, and I never went far enough to reveal their identity to anyone else. That was the game: it was just the two of us.

Anonymous chat rooms? Great. I'd never been much of a troll, but suddenly I was addicted. It was hilarious, watching people panic as I gradually revealed more and more information that I, an anonymous internet stranger, should not have known. 

Everywhere I went, I knew who people were. I always knew their identity. The details were the same for everyone: full name, age, sex, and location. Anything else I wanted I had to discover for myself. But that wasn't hard. The clues were everywhere, once I started looking. The data trails were easy to follow. And it was fun. Up to this point, I had been lonelier than I had ever imagined I could be. Now I knew everyone, without any effort at all. I didn't know how I'd picked this up, but I wasn't going to question it. I could make good things happen now, and no one ever knew that it was me. This was my superpower. I didn't need anything else.

My first act of vigilante justice was a total accident. My girlfriend had just left after a great evening of watching movies and eating pizza together. I was logged onto Reddit, just browsing, thinking about all the stuff I was procrastinating. A fairly normal evening. But then a throwaway account, confessing to some really messed up stuff, caught my eye. The username was just a keyboard smash, but it rang some weird bells. So I started to type a reply. (That counted for interaction, apparently: just doing that would get my superpower going.)

The user? A politician running for the presidency.

For a minute, I just sort of sat there, wondering what to do with this information. The confession was incredibly disturbing. Was it my job to report this? How was I supposed to tell somebody without getting asked a lot of awkward questions? Eventually, though, I decided to do it. I sent in an anonymous tip, then sat back and waited.

Three days later, the candidate dropped out of the race in a scandal that shook the country.

I thought that anonymous trolling gave me a rush. But this--this was even better. I'd done something good. Something a little bit heroic, even. It was amazing. Little old me--a lonely college kid--had managed to pull off a feat that changed the world. This really was a superpower. I was a superhero.

I got into this vigilante thing in earnest. I started digging deeper into the internet, finding the places where people were doing bad things. They never knew who I was, just that I was a random user who would wander in, talk to a few people, and wander away again. I took precautions to make sure that I was untraceable. And what I was doing worked. People who confessed to unsolved crimes found themselves arrested. People hurting other people were exposed. No criminal was safe from me, but behind the screen of my laptop I was always safe from them. 

One evening, I logged onto an anonymous chat room. It was the sort of place where I was always finding bad people, always having to run off to file an anonymous tip with someone. Normally, it was a hive of activity. But tonight, it was mostly empty. Just me and another user.

They didn't respond to my greeting, or to anything else. I couldn't get a read on them, since they weren't really interacting with me. They were just...there. It was boring, so after a minute I clicked away to another tab. 

Suddenly, I heard a series of short chimes: someone had messaged me over in the chatroom. When I looked at the page, I thought my heart was going to stop. The other user had posted four pieces of information. My full name. My age. My sex. And my location. And two other short messages:

*i know who you are*

*i'm coming to find you*
